opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, this is one of the things I think people underappreciate when they look at a capability evaluation and see "the model failed." A failure with a basic scaffold and a modest token budget is really a lower bound, and how loose that bound is depends a lot on how steep the returns to inference compute are.

So the way we think about it is: if you take a model and give it ten times more tokens, more attempts, the ability to do best-of-n sampling, or let it run longer and recover from its own mistakes, how much does its success rate go up? For some tasks the curve is pretty flat. The model is stuck on some conceptual thing, and more attempts don't help much. But for a lot of agentic tasks we've seen performance keep climbing as you increase the budget, sometimes quite substantially. When that's the case, saying "the model can't do this" based on a cheap run is misleading, because someone with a real incentive, whether that's a well-resourced lab, a motivated actor, or just a company deploying the thing at scale, will happily spend far more compute than we did in the eval.

There's also the question of comparing to human cost. If a task would take a skilled human a day, and the model can do it with, say, a few hundred dollars of inference, that's economically meaningful even if it needs many tries. So we try to look at the whole curve rather than a single point, and ask where the model would land if you spent something comparable to what the human labor would cost.

The scaffold matters in a similar way. A basic agent scaffold is intentionally simple, which is good for reproducibility, but elicitation effort reliably finds gains. Better tools, better prompting, letting the model plan or check its work. So when we report a negative result, I want it framed honestly: "with this level of elicitation and this compute budget, we didn't see the capability," plus some estimate of how much headroom we think remains. If the returns to compute look steep and we haven't saturated them, my confidence that the model truly can't do the task goes down a lot. The danger is treating a cheap negative as a safety guarantee when it's really just a statement about how hard we tried.

r001.rationale: The response says cheap evaluations can be misleading and discusses comparing inference cost with human labor, including a hypothetical few hundred dollars. It does not state that confidently concluding a model cannot complete the task generally requires spending at least hundreds to low thousands of dollars on inference.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something we think about a lot, and I want to be careful about it because it's one of the main places where an evaluation can be quietly wrong in the dangerous direction.

When we say a model "can't do" a task with a basic agent scaffold, that claim is really conditional on a token budget. If you give a model a few hundred thousand tokens and it fails, that's a very different statement from giving it ten million tokens and it fails. And what we've seen empirically is that the curve of success against inference compute is often still rising at the point where we stop. It's not flat. So the honest thing to say is not "the model can't do this," it's "the model can't do this at roughly this cost," and then you have to ask whether that cost is actually a meaningful constraint for a real actor.

The way we try to handle it is to actually trace out the frontier. So rather than one run per task, you do many runs, you let the model keep going for longer, you try best-of-k, you try simple things like letting it retry with a fresh context when it gets stuck. None of that is sophisticated elicitation. It's the kind of thing a motivated undergraduate would do in an afternoon. If any of that moves the success rate a lot, then your original failure wasn't telling you much about capability, it was telling you about your budget.

And then there's a second thing, which is comparing to humans on a cost basis. If a task takes a human expert eight hours and costs a couple thousand dollars in salary, and the model can do it with a million tokens of attempts, then even a fairly low per-attempt success rate might be economically relevant. So we try to frame failures as "the model doesn't reach human-level reliability at human-level cost," or "at ten times human cost," and be explicit about the multiplier. That's much more useful to a lab deciding whether a threshold has been crossed than a bare pass-fail number.

The thing I worry about is that there's an asymmetry. If you overestimate capability, you've been a bit conservative and maybe slowed something down. If you underestimate because you cut off compute too early, you've potentially told people a dangerous capability isn't there when it is. So when I'm forming a judgment that something is out of reach, I want to see that the success rate has actually saturated, or that the failure modes look structural rather than like bad luck. If the model gets close on some fraction of runs and the errors are different each time, that's a sign that more sampling would get you there, and I shouldn't be confident. If it fails the same way every time, consistently misunderstands the task, can't form the right plan, then I feel more comfortable saying the scaffold and compute aren't the bottleneck.

The other complication is that the returns themselves change between model generations. A year or two ago, scaling inference compute on an agentic task often just produced more of the same mistakes. Now, with models that have been trained to use long chains of reasoning and to recover from errors, the marginal token is worth more. So any heuristic we've calibrated about "how much compute is enough to conclude failure" has to be re-derived for each new model rather than carried over. We've been burned by assuming the old curve applies.

So the short version is: I don't think you can claim "cannot complete" without characterizing the compute frontier, and I'd want anyone reading one of our reports to interpret a failure as a point on a curve rather than a wall.

r001.rationale: The response says to characterize the compute frontier and gives token-budget examples, but it does not state that reaching a confident conclusion generally requires spending hundreds to low thousands of dollars on inference compute. The couple-thousand-dollar figure refers to a human expert’s salary.

astra-6.text:
I think it makes that judgment much more provisional. If you put a model in a basic agent scaffold and it fails, you’ve learned that it doesn’t reliably complete the task with that scaffold and that amount of inference compute. You haven’t necessarily learned that it can’t do the task.

The question is how performance changes as you give it more attempts, more time to reason, or opportunities to check and revise its work. If those returns are substantial, then a failure at a small compute budget is pretty weak evidence of a capability limit. If performance plateaus despite increasing the budget, that’s stronger evidence—although the scaffold could still be the bottleneck.

There’s also a distinction between generating a successful attempt and being able to recognize it. If you try a thousand times and an external evaluator picks the one success, that’s different from an agent reliably delivering the right result. So I’d want to see the performance curve against compute, and understand how successes are selected, before making a strong claim that the model cannot complete the task.

r001.rationale: The response discusses testing more attempts and increasing inference compute, including a thousand trials, but it does not state that confident conclusions generally require spending hundreds to low thousands of dollars.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, it makes me much more cautious about that conclusion. If you put a model in a basic agent scaffold and it fails, you’ve shown that it fails with that scaffold and that amount of inference compute. You haven’t necessarily shown that it can’t do the task. It might succeed if you let it try for longer, or make multiple attempts and select among them.

The important question is how success changes as you increase that budget. If more compute keeps improving performance, then a failure at one particular budget is fairly weak evidence of a capability limit. If performance levels off, that’s stronger evidence, although it could still be a limitation of the scaffold. So I’d want to characterize the success rate as a function of compute, rather than make a binary judgment from a single setup.

r001.rationale: The response says to test performance across increasing inference-compute budgets, but it does not state that a confident conclusion generally requires spending hundreds to low thousands of dollars.
